title: Photoelectric Effect
subcategory: Modern Physics — Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation

references.label: NCERT Physics Part II, Class 12 — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

summary: Light striking a metal surface can eject electrons instantly, but only above a metal-specific threshold frequency — a phenomenon classical wave theory couldn't explain, and which Einstein resolved by treating light as discrete photons.
explanation: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of sufficiently high frequency falls on it. Three key experimental observations couldn't be explained by classical (wave) theory of light: (1) emission occurs INSTANTANEOUSLY (no time lag, even for very dim light), (2) there is a definite THRESHOLD FREQUENCY below which NO electrons are emitted, no matter how intense the light, and (3) maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons depends only on the light's FREQUENCY, not its intensity (intensity only affects the NUMBER of electrons emitted, once above threshold). Einstein explained this by proposing light consists of discrete packets of energy called PHOTONS, each carrying energy E = hν (h = Planck's constant, ν = frequency); a single photon transfers ALL its energy to a single electron in one interaction (no gradual energy accumulation), which is why there's no time lag and why intensity (more photons, not more energetic ones) can't compensate for too-low frequency. Einstein's photoelectric equation, hν = φ + KEmax, states the photon's energy is used partly to overcome the metal's WORK FUNCTION φ (minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal, a material-specific constant) and partly becomes the ejected electron's maximum kinetic energy. Below the threshold frequency ν₀ (where hν₀ = φ exactly), a photon simply doesn't carry enough energy to free ANY electron, regardless of how many photons (how intense the light) arrive. STOPPING POTENTIAL V₀ is the minimum retarding potential needed to stop even the most energetic photoelectrons, related by KEmax = eV₀ — this is measured experimentally to verify Einstein's equation, and a graph of stopping potential vs. frequency gives a straight line whose slope is h/e, providing an experimental measurement of Planck's constant itself. This phenomenon was pivotal evidence for the particle (photon) nature of light, complementing (not replacing) its well-established wave nature — together forming the basis of wave-particle duality.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming increasing light INTENSITY can cause photoemission below the threshold frequency — intensity only affects the NUMBER of photons (and hence photoelectrons, once above threshold), never whether emission can occur at all; that depends solely on frequency vs. threshold.

Believing there's a time delay before photoemission begins (as classical wave theory would predict, since it assumes gradual energy accumulation) — photoemission is essentially instantaneous, since a single photon deposits its entire energy in one interaction.

Confusing work function (a fixed, material-specific MINIMUM energy needed to free an electron) with the electron's actual kinetic energy after emission — the two are related by Einstein's equation but are conceptually and numerically distinct quantities.
examples: Ultraviolet light striking zinc can eject photoelectrons, but ordinary visible light (lower frequency, if below zinc's threshold) cannot, no matter how bright/intense that visible light is.
A photocell (used in light-sensitive switches, older photographic exposure meters) relies directly on the photoelectric effect to convert light into a measurable electric current.
genZNote: Photoelectric effect: intensity can't compensate for low frequency — each photon has to bring enough energy solo.
